# Digest R7 — 2 Pet 2:17–3:7 (L3235–3439)

Tags: `2-peter`, `gene-green`, `1-peter`, `peter-apostle`, `green-jude-2peter-becnt`, `new-creation`

## Coverage

- **Source:** Gene L. Green, *Jude and 2 Peter* (BECNT) — cache slice `R7-2pet-2_17-3_7.txt`
- **Line range read:** L3235–3439 (file-internal markers 3235–3439)
- **Text covered:** 2 Peter 2:17–22 (waterless springs / mists; grand empty speech; promise of freedom; last state worse than first; dog/sow maxims; apostasy) and 3:1–7 (second letter as reminder; prophets and apostles; scoffers in last days; “Where is the promise?”; fathers; creation-by-word; flood; present heavens/earth reserved for fire)
- **Not read beyond range:** 3:8–10 section header and preview only (L3433–3435) — claims limited to what Green states within range about delay; no full exegesis of 3:8–10
- **Evidence class:** modern critical/exegetical commentary (Green’s apparatus and exegesis), not primary NT text alone

## Claims

### 2:17–22 seduction and apostasy

1. **Green: Peter reworks Jude 12–13 for waterless springs / storm-driven mists.** Green attributes: “Peter redoubles his effort in denouncing the heretics, once again drawing on Jude as his source, which he adapts to his own ends… specifically drawing on Jude 12–13.” Instead of Jude’s “clouds without rain,” “Peter refers to the heretics as waterless springs”; Jude’s wind-driven clouds become “mists driven by the storm”; 2 Pet 2:17 “borrows the phrase almost exactly” of Jude 13’s gloom of darkness, “leaving out only εἰς αἰῶνα (… forever)” and not coupling it with wild waves / wandering stars. (L3241)

2. **Green: “These are” reopens denunciation after Balaam.** Green: “Peter begins his second round of denunciations of the heretics with the rhetorical marker οὗτοί εἰσιν… which not only signals a new paragraph but also turns attention back to the heretics after the comparison with Balaam in the preceding verses (2:15–16).” (L3243)

3. **Green: Waterless spring = promise without produce.** Green: “For those who walk the length of Palestine and other arid lands, nothing can be more dreadful than a spring without water… This type of spring is filled with promise but because of drought produces nothing (Jer. 14:3).” (L3243)

4. **Green: Mists = unproductive / foreboding, not pleasant dew.** Green cites Aristotle: “Mist is the residue of the condensation of air into water… mist is as it were unproductive cloud”; Peter’s mists “produce foreboding darkness… like the classic London fog of a Sherlock Holmes tale,” “whipped up” by storm/tempest. Charge “may be that the heretics are incapable of producing anything of value through their teachings, despite their grand promises (2:19).” (L3245)

5. **Green alternative: metaphors of deadness and doom.** Green: “The metaphors… likely refer to the spiritual state of the heretics, which eventuates in their ultimate judgment. These people are dead and destined for doom.” (L3247)

6. **Green: Gloom of darkness = reserved nether judgment.** Green: “The ‘gloom’… is the place where the fallen angels are bound until the day of judgment (2:4…)… The description of this ‘gloom’ as ‘darkness’ indicates that the place of judgment and torment is outside the kingdom… As the angels are kept under judgment… so the darkness of the nether gloom is kept… for the heretics. This will be their final end… Such people are lost, beyond the limits of salvation.” (L3249)

7. **Green: 2:18 γάρ grounds judgment in community conduct.** Green: Peter “returns to the topic of the conduct of the heretics amid the Christian community, which, he explains, is the reason for their coming judgment (the sentence begins with γάρ… which marks the cause or reason for the preceding).” (L3251)

8. **Green: Heretics entice recent converts with sex and empty grand speech.** Green’s reading of 2:18: “The false teachers are arrogant and seek to entice recent converts into their error through the promise of sexual gratification… ‘For by uttering enormous empty things, they entice with the licentious desires of the flesh those who have only recently escaped from the ones who live in error.’” (L3251)

9. **Green: Jude 16 adapted — high-sounding speech + sexual bait.** Green: “Peter draws on Jude 16… Both authors censure the overblown speech of the heretics (ὑπέρογκα) and highlight their aggressive attempts to gain converts. Jude comments that the heretics use flattery… while Peter tags their persuasive power as both high-sounding speech and sexual bait, which wiggles on the hook.” (L3251)

10. **Green: Grand speech is empty/false — sound without substance.** Green on ὑπέρογκα… ματαιότητος: “he categorizes their boast as nothing, being empty or vain… The term also suggests falsity since there is no reality to their claims… There is sound but no substance.” (L3253)

11. **Green: Targets are recent converts still unstable.** Green: objects are “those who have ‘scarcely escaped’… Previously Peter used the language of escape as a descriptor of the divine act of salvation… Peter observes that these have ‘recently’ escaped… The recent converts are, in his eyes, unstable still.” (L3255)

12. **Green: “Those who live in error” = unconverted pagan body, not yet the heretics’ doctrinal error alone.** Green: “Peter’s thought in the present verse is not that the heretics have erred from the truth. Here he lumps the body of the unconverted together as ‘those who live in error.’” (L3257)

13. **Green: Bait is licentious fleshly desire; vice dressed as virtue at agapē.** Green: “What they are, however, is what they promise. Sex is at the very heart of the problem… The heretics advocate a return to this loose pagan lifestyle… Amazingly, they throw out this bait as they gather with the church, turning the agapē meals into times of revelry and lust (2:13–14…). They seek ‘to dress up vice as virtue’ (M. Green 1987: 128).” (L3259)

14. **Green: Carpocratian parallel is second-century; 2 Peter heretics not fully gnostic.** Green: “during the second century AD the gnostic sect known as the Carpocratians promoted liberty and sexual license… characteristic features of gnostic thought such as dualism and the creation of the world by a demiurge are apparently not tenets of the false teachers’ appeal that Peter counters.” (L3261)

15. **Green: Epicurean-flavored merge is attractive but eclectic, not pure Epicureanism.** Green: “The suggestion that false teachers in 2 Peter had merged Christian with Epicurean thought is surely attractive… since that philosophy not only denied the possibility of future judgment but also elevated desires (ἐπιθυμίαι) to the level of virtue, both features that mark the heretics.” Yet “we are pressed hard to imagine how Epicurean thought could have gained any foothold in the church since Epicureans believed that the gods were not involved… However, the first century was a period in which disparate religious and philosophical traditions could be patched together… Eclecticism was well established… The trends that the heretics reflect are not difficult to identify but the exact nature of their belief may well defy systemization. Certainly the affirmation of bodily gratification was an appealing notion and, coupled with an exaltation of freedom (2:19), would put a very attractive, although lurid, spin on the apostolic faith.” (L3263)

16. **Green: Promise of freedom is hallmark of heretics’ appeal; irony = slaves of moral corruption.** Green on 2:19: “A hallmark of their philosophy is the promise of freedom… ‘Although they promise them freedom, they themselves are slaves of corruption.’” On φθορά: “the term may also refer to moral corruption… and this is certainly the sense here. The present context places emphasis on issues of morality (2:15–16, 18).” (L3265)

17. **Green surveys “freedom” options; rejects gnostic archons and political freedom.** Green via Bauckham’s list: freedom from moral law; Gnostic freedom from archons/demiurge; freedom from perishability; political freedom; freedom from fear of Parousia judgment. Green: gnostic intermediary freedom “is unlikely” (no dualism); Reicke’s politically aggressive heretics is “mere conjecture”; φθορά here is moral not mortality. Pauline-liberty-into-vice is “plausibly interpreted within this frame”; freedom-from-judgment-fear is “attractive if we understand the heretics to be people who are influenced by the Epicurean notion that the gods do not intervene… and that delay in divine vengeance is evidence that there will be no future judgment.” (L3265–3267)

18. **Green: Freedom was philosophical commonplace (Epicurean, Stoic, skeptic) — not a school marker alone.** Green: “The promise of freedom, however, was a philosophical commonplace and is not, in and of itself, a marker for any particular school of thought. Epicureans, Stoics, and skeptics alike discussed human freedom and promised the same.” (L3269) Green elaborates Lucian, Seneca, Epictetus, Epicurus’s anti-determinism / atomic swerve, Carneades, Chrysippus — “‘Freedom’ was a dominant topos.” (L3271–3273)

19. **Green: Heretics sanction desire like Epicureans but remain eclectic theists in the church.** Green: “While they apparently make appeal to Paul, their notion of freedom is not fully understandable as a perversion of Paul’s teaching. Their sanctioning of desire (v. 18) is similar to Epicurean thought but… their presence in the church and theism suggest an eclectic system not fully compatible with Epicurean thought.” (L3275)

20. **Green: Irony — cannot offer what one does not have; 2:20–22 = apostasy as evidence of enslavement.** Green: “The irony of their promise is the fact that one cannot offer what one does not have. The following verses (2:20–22) describe the apostasy of the heretics, which is evidence of their enslavement… The one who is given over to sin is its slave. No slave can promise freedom.” Corruption “is most likely sexual in nature.” (L3275)

21. **Green: Aphorism of conquest → slavery (military slave source).** Green on ᾧ γάρ τις ἥττηται, τούτῳ δεδούλωται: “appealing to what appears to be an aphorism… Bauckham… notes that the proverb was widely quoted by Christian authors… The allusion refers to military conquest, which was the source of numerous slaves… Having been vanquished by sin, they are now its slaves.” (L3277)

22. **Green: Subjects of 2:20 are the heretics (apostates), not the duped recent converts.** Green weighs both options but concludes: “the topic of the paragraph running from verse 17 is the heretics themselves… Moreover, the explanatory γάρ… suggests that we understand the present verse as elaborating his point about the apostasy of the false teachers… Our author uses the same verb in verse 20… lest there be any confusion regarding to whom he refers.” (L3279)

23. **Green: Escape from “defilements of the world” = moral-boundary vices, via personal knowledge of Lord and Savior.** Green: “The ‘defilements’… are acts that cross the moral boundary… Such immoral deeds are characteristic of the world… Such change… has come about ‘in the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ’… The ‘knowledge’… is that which brings conversion and salvation… As elsewhere, the knowledge is personal. Its object is Jesus Christ… They had obtained entrance into his eternal kingdom (1:11)… their present apostasy is the height of hubris as well as an unfathomable tragedy.” (L3281–3283)

24. **Green: Re-entanglement = genuine apostasy with no escape.** Green: “The heretics have become ‘entangled’ again… The term… suggests not only involvement in an activity but also entrapment… This is genuine apostasy, from which there is no escape… The heretics have turned from ‘the holy commandment’ (2:21) and denied ‘the Master who bought them’ (2:1).” (L3287)

25. **Green: “Last state worse than first” echoes Jesus (Matt 12:43–45 // Luke 11:24–26) and early apostasy instruction.** Green: “The sentence echoes the teaching of Jesus… The statement of Jesus may itself be a traditional proverb… Jesus’s teaching was woven into the fabric of early Christian instruction regarding apostasy… Herm. Sim. 9.17.5… so conceptually similar to 2 Pet. 2:20 that the present epistle likely served as Hermas’s source.” (L3289)

26. **Green: Worse last state — better never to have known (v. 21); judgment/damnation in view.** Green: “Peter does not discuss here how the apostates’ last state… is worse than the first, except in stating that it would have been better not to know the way of righteousness than to know it and turn back (v. 21)… But previously Peter has underscored the divine judgment that would come on such people (2:1), the worse state in view being the sentence of damnation.” (L3291)

27. **Green: 2:21 is Tob-Spruch (“better… than”) form with proverbial ring.** Green: “which has a distinctly proverbial ring… Walther Zimmerli (1933) dubbed this kind of proverbial declaration… a ‘Tob-Spruch’… We should not conclude that our author draws on a known proverb at this point, however, but the form he employs will ring as a wisdom saying.” (L3293)

28. **Green: Superior state = never knowing the way than knowing and returning.** Green: “Our author therefore makes the stunning observation that the superior state would be not to have known the ‘way’ at all than, having known it, to return to the former way of life. In Peter’s view, one should not come if one does not expect to stay… The more severe judgment will come on the one who knows.” (L3295)

29. **Green: Knowing the Lord entails “the way of righteousness” — ethical dimension inseparable.** Green: “The heretics have not only known the Lord but have also known ‘the way of righteousness,’ implying that knowing the Lord entails embracing a righteous way of life. The ethical dimension of the relationship with Christ cannot be set aside.” (L3297)

30. **Green: “Holy commandment” = gospel demand handed down as sacred tradition (cf. 3:2).** Green: “This is the commandment ‘of the Lord and Savior given through your apostles,’ which was proclaimed to them in the gospel (3:2…)… The gospel is not simply an offer; it is a demand that must be obeyed… On this reading, the ‘holy commandment’ would be the substance of the initial Christian instruction that new converts receive… a sacred tradition divinely inspired (see Jude 3…). To turn away the divine imperative… is indeed a state worse than never having heard the sacred command.” (L3303)

31. **Green: Dog maxim from Prov 26:11; unclean return to left-behind evil.** Green: first maxim “is drawn from Prov. 26:11… The heretics were no better than dogs who, having once disgorged… return to eat what they left… Peter’s application… is that the heretics have returned to the evil they left behind… Proverbs 26:11 tags this as behavior characteristic of the ‘fool’… Peter concurs.” (L3309)

32. **Green: Sow maxim — washed then returns to mud; genuine apostasy.** Green prefers reading “as the dog returns, so the sow returns to the filth… This is what the apostate heretics have done (v. 21)… They, once having known the Lord and his holy commandment, have denied the Lord (2:1), have been entangled in the defilements of the world again (2:20), and have turned away after having known the way of righteousness (2:21), forgetting that they had been purified from past sins (1:9). This is genuine apostasy… Peter holds out no hope for such ‘beasts.’” (L3311)

33. **Green textual note on 2:18 ὀλίγως vs ὄντως.** Green Additional Note: “Although numerous MSS read ὄντως… the reading ὀλίγως is that of the Alexandrian and Western families and finds very early testimony in 𝔓72… It is unlikely that an exchange of a rare word for a common one would have been made.” (L3316)

### 3:1–2 reminder; prophets and apostles

34. **Green: 3:1–18a is body closing — Call to Holiness; structure of scoffers, flood type, delay, ethics.** Green: “Our author introduces the final section of the letter, the body closing… After these introductory words our author identifies the heretics, noting that they are controlled by desire (v. 3) and that they deny that God will intervene to judge the world (3:3–7)… Peter explains the reason for their skepticism as the apparent lack of divine judgment in the past (v. 4), but at once counters their claim with an appeal to the history of divine judgment (vv. 5–6), which serves as the type of the judgment to come (v. 7).” (L3335)

35. **Green: Epicurean identification of denial-of-judgment is main evidence, but position more eclectic.** Green: “Their denial of future judgment due to divine delay in judgment in the past has been one of the main evidences forwarded to identify these teachers as people who have embraced aspects of Epicurean thought. However, the skepticism that the heretics evidence is not limited to the Epicureans, and their position appears to be more eclectic than is sometimes recognized.” (L3335)

36. **Green: 3:1–2 = second major “reminder” topos of moral philosophy.** Green: “This is the second major ‘reminder’ of the letter (see 1:12–15) as Peter evokes this common topos in moral philosophy of reminding one’s hearers/readers of what they already know in order to ensure their moral progress.” (L3343)

37. **Green: “Beloved” = familial solidarity against heretics.** Green: “Throughout this section he returns to address them… (3:8, 14, 17)… The use of ‘beloved’ within the early church was a marker of the familial relationship… They are those who are inside, within the circle of the family, and not those separated off, as were the heretics.” (L3354)

38. **Green: “Second letter” elevates present teaching as confirming sequence.** Green: “The opening words… Ταύτην ἤδη… sometimes appear at the head of numbered sequences… The emphasis is on the way the second or third in the sequence serves as a confirmation of the previous… Peter’s comment that this is his second letter confirms the content of the first epistle but, at the same time, highlights the importance of the present teaching. In fact, it elevates the importance of this letter above the first.” (L3356)

39. **Green: Previous letter = 1 Peter (not Jude, not a lost letter).** Green: “There is little doubt that the previous letter is the book known to us as 1 Peter.” Against Robinson (Jude as first): “no plausible explanation can overcome the simple fact that Jude is not attributed to Peter.” Against M. Green’s lost-letter view: 1 Peter does remind (1 Pet 1:12; 2:2; 1:18); 2 Pet 1:12, 16 “do not necessarily imply that Peter had a personal ministry among the readers.” (L3358)

40. **Green: Both letters share end of rousing pure understanding by reminder.** Green: “the author of 2 Peter wishes to underscore the commonality of the two documents… He states that both this and the previous correspondence have the same end… Peter seeks to preserve the singularity and simplicity of their understanding and does not want to see it sullied in any way by the persuasion of the heretics and their error… To call both 1 and 2 Peter reminders of such teaching is wholly in line with the purposes of both letters.” (L3362)

41. **Green: 3:2 adapts Jude 17 by adding holy prophets + “commandment… through your apostles.”** Green: “Peter’s language is nearly identical to his source, Jude 17… Instead of including Jude’s exhortation to remember apostolic teaching, Peter states that his purpose is to remind them so that they will recall the prophetic testimony as well as the apostolic teaching… Peter has already stated… that the teaching… is well founded on both faithful apostolic testimony (1:16–18) and a sure prophetic word (1:19–21).” (L3364)

42. **Green: “Holy prophets” = OT prophets, not NT-era prophets.** Green against Sidebottom: “in light of Peter’s previous teaching about the veracity of the prophetic message of the OT (1:19–21), which the false teachers have cast in doubt, we should understand these ‘holy prophets’ as messengers known to us through the OT… we should understand the ‘words previously spoken by the holy prophets’ in the same manner here.” (L3368)

43. **Green: “Your apostles” = those who proclaimed the message to them (incl. probably Paul); not subapostolic marker.** Green: “The ‘commandment’ is the same one referred to in 2:21… the ‘holy commandment’ or the substance of apostolic instruction… ‘Your apostles’ are simply those who have proclaimed the Christian message to them. Paul was probably one of this company (3:15)… The reference to ‘your apostles’ is not a sign that this document comes from the subapostolic era… nor is Peter trying to distinguish between true apostles and false apostles with the pronoun ‘your’… For the church to maintain its identity, it cannot abandon the prophetic and apostolic testimony.” (L3370)

### 3:3–7 scoffers; flood; reserved for fire

44. **Green: Debate frame — immutability of world vs divine judgment; Peter stands on revelation.** Green section intro: “In this section Peter enters into a debate current in his day about the immutability of the world and the possibility of divine judgment. His perspective is not shaped principally by philosophical currents but by the witness of the prophets and the Lord handed down through the apostles.” (L3378)

45. **Green: 3:3 “above all know this” = presence of mockers as last-days sign (predicted, already present).** Green: “Peter’s focus in the present verse… is on the presence of the heretics as a sign that the last days have arrived. The readers should be fully aware that their coming was predicted… Like Jude, Peter recognizes the presence of the heretics as a sign that the last days have arrived… His focus is not on some future time but on his own days.” (L3389, L3393)

46. **Green: Mockers live by own desires; root of heresy is moral, not intellectual.** Green: “These people are… ‘living according to their own desires’… Not virtue but base desires govern the conduct of the heretics… The root of their heresy is moral, not intellectual. The doubts about the promise of Christ’s coming and the future judgment (2 Pet. 3:4) are framed by reason and experience, but their true source is the base character of the heretics. The doctrinal denial warrants their behavior, but their character and praxis give rise to their skepticism. Heteropraxis begets heterodoxy.” (L3393–3395)

47. **Green: Scoffers’ question “Where is the promise of his coming?” is classic skeptical form.** Green: “introducing a question with the words ‘Where is’ was common among those whom we may broadly classify as skeptics… The question of the false teachers is a demand for evidence regarding ‘the promise of his coming’… The heretics have given their own promise of ‘freedom’ (2:19) but at the same time place in doubt the divine promises… But the heretics bring into doubt these promises, which came through divine revelation, basing their skepticism on their own empirical assessment of history: such is the height of their hubris.” (L3397)

48. **Green: Heretics question not only advent but judgment he ushers in.** Green: “the heretics question not only the reality of Christ’s advent but also the judgment that he will usher in, as is evident from Peter’s response in verses 5–10. Peter understands this connection well and stands with the dominical teaching that joins Christ’s advent with his judgment of the nations.” (L3399)

49. **Green: “Fathers” = ancestors in general (long past), not first Christian generation.** Green: “The ‘fathers’ has sometimes been taken as a reference to the first generation of Christians… especially attractive if the author is identified not as Peter but rather as a second-generation or later Christian writing under his name… However, the early church did not refer to the first generation of Christians in this way… Likely the reference is to ‘ancestors’ in general since the heretics are simply making a point about time long past and conditions that have not changed since then.” (L3403)

50. **Green: Heretics claim permanence from creation; Green parallels Epicurus / Diogenes of Oenoanda.** Green: heretics affirm “all things remain as they were from the beginning of creation… Their doctrine is similar to the claims of Epicurus: ‘But, in truth, the universal whole always was such as it now is, and always will be such…’ … Diogenes of Oenoanda stated… ‘these things are absolutely indestructible…’ The heretics’ argument is that God has not intervened in human history, empirical evidence showing that all things continue without change… The promises of God have not come to pass in the past, nor will they come to pass in the future. This is the foundation of their skepticism and mocking of the apostolic teaching regarding the promises of God (2 Pet. 2:3).” (L3405)

51. **Green: Chiastic structure A/B/B′/A′ for 3:4–10.** Green cites Bauckham: “the structure of these verses is chiastic: A (3:4a), B (3:4b), B′ (3:5–7), A′ (3:8–10).” (L3407)

52. **Green: Heretics willfully ignore creation/sustenance by God’s word.** Green: “Peter does not tag the false teachers simply as those who have failed to take note of some fundamental truths. Rather, they are people who have ignored or willfully passed over them… Their ignorance is not merely an unfortunate circumstance. They are marked as those who have willfully passed over the fundamental truths from Scripture that Peter now elaborates.” (L3407)

53. **Green: Heavens came into being long ago by God’s word; earth sustained by same word.** Green: “The creation of the heavens and the earth by the ‘word of God’ is a fundamental and oft-repeated theme… He turns his attention to the earth… which exists or is sustained… by this very same divine word… the earth endures or is held together by this very word… Peter’s affirmation echoes that of Heb. 1:3… and anticipates his claim in 3:7 that ‘by the same word the present heavens and earth have been reserved for fire.’” (L3409–3411)

54. **Green: Concedes stability, but stability is divine agency — same word reserves world for judgment.** Green: “The heretics have rejected divine revelation by asserting that all things have remained the same from creation. Peter, in part, concedes their point… Things have indeed continued the same from creation until the present. But this stability, as the creation, is due to divine agency. And that same agency, the word of God, sustains the present world for the future judgment (3:7). The heretics have diminished God’s word, questioning his promises (3:4).” (L3411)

55. **Green: Earth formed “out of water and through water” (Gen 1:6–10 tradition); water then destroyed the world.** Green: “he notes, parenthetically, that the creation of the earth was… ‘having been formed out of water and through water’… He alludes to Gen. 1:6–10… The earth came out of water, but the water turned and destroyed the earth (3:6). God, the sustainer of the earth, is also the judge of the earth.” (L3413)

56. **Green: Flood (3:6) cuts heart of “all things remain” claim and types future judgment.** Green: “By recalling the flood, our author cuts the heart out of the heretics’ claim that ‘all things remain as they were from the beginning of creation’ (3:4b) and at the same time lays the foundation for his assertion… that God will indeed judge the world in the future, just as he has done in the past… ‘the world at that time was destroyed, being flooded by water’… Peter’s end here is to show that the flood is an example of God’s intervention to judge the world.” (L3415)

57. **Green: Creative waters became agency of destruction — God reversed creative act.** Green: “the very waters out of which and through which the world was created (2 Pet. 3:5) became the agency for the destruction of the world of that time… God reversed his creative act as the waters that brought forth the world also brought that world to its end.” (L3417)

58. **Green: Three worlds — antediluvian, present, world to come (new-creation foreshadow).** Green: “Peter refers to three worlds in this letter: the antediluvian (3:6), the present (3:7), and the world to come (3:13). Just as the first world was brought into being and sustained by the word of God (3:5), so also the present world is sustained by that very same word (3:7). But as the first world was destroyed (3:6), so too the second will end in a cataclysmic divine judgment (3:7, 10–12), after which God will usher in the world to come (3:13).” (L3419)

59. **Green: Present heavens and earth reserved for fire by same word; kept for day of judgment and destruction of ungodly.** Green translates/expounds 3:7: “‘but by the same word the present heavens and earth have been reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly people’… As prisoners awaiting the execution of the judgment pronounced upon them, so the present world is reserved for that final day. Divine providence extends down to judgment.” (L3419–3421)

60. **Green: Means of future judgment is fire not water; OT/NT/Jewish fire judgment; L.A.E. joins flood then fire.** Green: “The means of judgment will be ‘fire’… and not water, as in the flood… Previously Peter spoke of the judgment of Sodom and Gomorrah, which were turned to ash (2:6…), and that judgment by fire presaged the one to come… The first-century-AD L.A.E. 49.3 joins together the judgment by flood and fire… ‘first by water and then by fire.’” (L3423)

61. **Green: Stoic ἐκπύρωσις is parallel-sounding but not Peter’s cosmology; linear three-world scheme, transcendent God.** Green: “The Stoics also spoke of the judgment of the world by fire, but the roots of Peter’s declaration are markedly Judeo-Christian… His cosmology, however, is different from Stoic doctrine since God is transcendent and the creative word of God brings the world into being. The same God will bring in the new order of heaven and earth. Peter does not share Stoic cyclicism but understands that there are three worlds: the past, the present, and the future. God is the one who creates, sustains, judges, and then re-creates without any suggestion that the process is anything other than linear.” (L3425)

62. **Green: Day of judgment = day of the Lord / day of God marked by advent; personal consequences for ungodly.** Green: “The ‘day of judgment’ (2:9; 1:19…) is also called ‘the day of the Lord’ (3:10) and ‘the day of God’ (3:12), the very day that is marked by the advent of the Lord Jesus… That ‘day’ will bring the ‘destruction’… on those who reject that way of God, those who are here described as ‘ungodly people’… The judgment of the world has personal consequences.” (L3427)

### Additional Notes

63. **Structural bookkeeping (Green’s outline within range).** Green labels: Body Closing: A Call to Holiness (3:1–18a); “1. A Call to Remember Prophetic and Apostolic Teaching (3:1–2)”; “2. Understand This: The Scoffers of the Last Day (3:3–7)”; next unit starts “3. Do Not Ignore This: One Day Is as a Thousand Years (3:8–10)” — only the transition preview is in range (L3328–3333, L3341, L3376, L3433–3435).

64. **Preview of delay explanation (boundary only).** Within range Green previews that after refuting “all things continue without change,” Peter must explain apparent delay: God’s time vs human calculation (v. 8); day comes like a thief (v. 10a); delay as mercy desiring salvation not destruction (v. 9); judgment still comes (v. 10). Full exegesis of 3:8–10 is **outside** declared range. (L3435)

65. **Authorship/relationship asides (Green records positions).** Green notes ancient stylistic doubts about 2 Peter authenticity; modern assessments of 1–2 Peter relationship diverge (Boobyer/Bigg vs Gilmore); he does not adjudicate authorship in this pericope beyond using “Peter” for the author and affirming 3:1 points to 1 Peter. (L3360)

## Claim count

**65 claims** (slightly above 40–60 target to cover dense freedom/Epicurean and creation–flood–fire blocks without dropping mandated themes). All claims attributed to **Gene L. Green** with verbatim anchors and L-line loci from the assigned cache slice only.
